about: The guidebook: the principles, concerns, methods, data rules and known limits every finding is cited against, the concern ladder, and the steps of the algorithm with the entries they apply and the tables they need. Each entry states its basis; 'Administration policy' marks a choice the administration owns, not an external rule. Method definitions are numbered MD-1, MD-2 and so on, so they are never mistaken for Traficom's regulations, such as M4, the national frequency allocation table.

sections.about: What Tosi does not cover yet, said plainly.

entries.title: Nothing is made up
entries.rule: Every number Tosi shows comes from one of three places: something written in the filing itself, a value in a published table, or a calculation whose formula is written down. No language model, and no system that learns from examples, is involved in producing any result.
entries.why: When Finland raises a concern with another country, that country's engineers will check every number. If a number came from a model that guesses, nobody could explain where it came from, and the concern would fall apart. A number that comes from a stated formula can be checked step by step by anyone.
entries.effect: Anything Tosi reports can be opened up to show where it came from: the row in the filing, the limit in the published table, or the formula that was used.

entries.title: The same file always gives the same answer
entries.rule: If the same file is processed twice, with the same rules, Tosi gives exactly the same result both times. Every result also records a fingerprint of the file it came from, a short code computed from the file's contents.
entries.why: If two runs of the same file could disagree, nobody would know which one to trust. The fingerprint also proves, long afterwards, exactly which file a result was based on. Change a single letter in the file and the fingerprint changes completely.
entries.effect: Results can be compared exactly, down to the last character, and each one says which file and which version of the rules produced it.

entries.title: People make the decisions
entries.rule: Tosi finds possible problems, measures them and shows the evidence. A person with the right expertise decides what to do about each one. Tosi never contacts anyone or sends anything on its own.
entries.why: Deciding whether to object to another country's filing is a judgement between administrations, and someone has to be responsible for it. Software can search, calculate and explain, but it cannot carry that responsibility.
entries.effect: Any letter Tosi prepares is a draft. The process always stops at a person, who reads the evidence and decides.

entries.title: Extra checks by AI stay separate
entries.rule: An AI system may be used, separately, to look over the results and suggest things that might have been missed. What it produces is only a list of suggestions for people to read. It cannot create a finding, change one, or change the order in which findings are ranked.
entries.why: Rules only catch what someone thought to write down, so a second look can find gaps. But that second look can also be wrong, so it must never be able to change a result directly.
entries.effect: A suggestion goes onto a list for review. It only has an effect if a person accepts it and it becomes a new or changed rule, through the normal review.

entries.title: Rules change only after review
entries.rule: A rule can only change through a proposal. The proposal is tested on past files, approved by a person, and saved as a new version of the guidebook. Nothing can quietly rewrite the rules while Tosi is in use.
entries.why: Regulations, data and priorities change over time, so the rules must be able to change too. But if a rule changed without anyone noticing, old and new results could no longer be compared, and nobody could say why a result had changed.
entries.effect: Before anyone approves a change, its effect on real past results is shown, so the decision is made knowing exactly what it will change.

entries.title: What counts as a concern
entries.rule: A filing is a concern if the signal it would put over Finland is above the allowed limit. It is also a concern if the signal is just under the limit, or if a strong signal falls very close to a frequency that Finland uses and protects.
entries.why: A limit gives a yes-or-no answer, but real interference doesn't work like that. A filing just under the limit is one small change away from breaking it. And a strong signal just outside a Finnish frequency can still leak into a nearby receiver. So Tosi looks a little wider than the strict limit.
entries.effect: Every filing is placed on the concern ladder. Clear breaches of the limit go at the top; near misses are placed below them.

entries.title: How close counts as close
entries.rule: A result within 3 decibels of the limit is treated as close to the limit. (A difference of 3 decibels means roughly double or half the power.)
entries.why: Filings are often modified after they are first published, and every calculation carries a little uncertainty. A result that is only a factor of two away from the limit should not be treated as safely clear.
entries.effect: This 3-decibel margin is a choice made by the administration, not an international rule. It is kept in one place, so it can be changed and its effect tested.

entries.title: Powerful antennas pointing at a satellite
entries.rule: If a Finnish station has a strongly focused antenna (a gain of at least 20 dBi, meaning it collects about a hundred times more signal from the direction it points) and that direction includes a satellite that stays fixed in the sky, the level at which Tosi raises a concern is lowered by 6 decibels.
entries.why: A focused antenna gathers far more energy from wherever it points. A satellite that sits inside that direction can cause harm even when its signal is below the general limit. Because a fixed-position satellite never moves, Tosi can work out exactly whether an antenna is pointing at it.
entries.effect: For each such station, Tosi works out the angle between where the antenna points and where the satellite is, and compares it with how wide the antenna's beam is. Satellites that move across the sky are not tested this way, because they don't stay in any antenna's beam.

entries.title: What Tosi protects
entries.rule: Frequencies that Finnish stations receive on are protected. Frequencies they transmit on are protected too, because whatever is transmitted is received by someone in Finland. Broadcasting is protected across the whole area it covers, not just at the transmitter.
entries.why: Finland's use of the radio spectrum isn't only where a receiver happens to be listed. Radio listeners, television viewers and the far end of a radio link are all receivers, even when the register only lists the transmitter.
entries.effect: A Finnish station is matched against a filing using both its receive and its transmit frequencies.

entries.title: Assume the worst for satellites
entries.rule: Tosi works out how much power from a satellite would arrive on each square metre of ground in Finland (called power flux density). It assumes the satellite's antenna is aimed straight at Finland at full strength, whatever the filing says about where it points. The result is an upper bound, not a forecast.
entries.why: Public filings don't reliably say where a satellite's beams point, and satellites can change where they point. Assuming the worst can sometimes raise a false alarm, but it will never hide a real problem.
entries.effect: If a filing passes this test, it passes everywhere. If it fails, it may still be fine in practice, so a person takes a closer look.

entries.title: Which limits apply to satellites
entries.rule: The limits on how much satellite power may arrive on the ground, which frequency bands they cover, and how they depend on the angle the signal arrives from, are taken from the international Radio Regulations, using the tables the ITU publishes.
entries.why: These limits are agreed between countries, and using the ITU's own tables avoids copying mistakes. They depend on the angle of arrival because ground antennas mostly look towards the horizon, so signals arriving at a low angle do more harm.
entries.effect: Tosi checks the limit at every arrival angle and keeps the one where the satellite comes closest to breaking it.

entries.title: Comparing power on the same footing
entries.rule: Before comparing with a limit, the power stated in the filing is converted to the same slice of frequency the limit is written for, using the method in the ITU's technical annex.
entries.why: Limits are written for a fixed slice of frequency, such as 4 kilohertz or 1 megahertz, while filings may give total power or power spread over a different width. Without converting, the two numbers can't be compared fairly.
entries.effect: The filed power is converted first, and only then compared with the limit.

entries.title: Which ground stations are checked
entries.rule: The check on stations on the ground covers land mobile radio only: base stations (class FB) and mobile stations (class ML), as listed in the ITU's terrestrial preface.
entries.why: The European threshold used to decide when neighbours need to coordinate was written for land mobile radio. Applying it to other kinds of service would produce numbers that look precise but don't mean much.
entries.effect: Other kinds of station, such as fixed links, are left out of this check, and the reason is recorded.

entries.title: How a signal travels over land and sea
entries.rule: The strength of a signal from a foreign station is worked out with the ITU's standard method for this (Recommendation P.1546-6). It is calculated for the signal level reached 10% of the time, at half of all locations, for a receiving antenna 10 metres above the ground, without using a detailed map of the terrain.
entries.why: Close to the ground, radio signals don't simply weaken with distance in a fixed way; they depend on the path, the land and the weather. P.1546 is the internationally agreed way to estimate this. Using the level reached 10% of the time captures the occasional strong conditions that actually cause interference.
entries.effect: The calculation is run for each border point, using the power and antenna height stated in the filing.

entries.title: When neighbours need to talk
entries.rule: A foreign station is a concern if the signal it would put at the Finnish border is above the European trigger level for its frequency band (from recommendation T/R 25-08), adjusted for how wide its channel is.
entries.why: This trigger level is what European countries have agreed: below it, neighbours don't need to coordinate. Wider channels pick up more power, so the level is adjusted for them.
entries.effect: The calculated signal at the border is compared with the trigger level for that band.

entries.title: Frequencies above 470 MHz
entries.rule: Above 470 MHz, the trigger level the recommendation gives for frequencies above 400 MHz is used.
entries.why: The recommendation's table stops at 470 MHz, but many land mobile filings use higher frequencies. Carrying the last value forward gives a consistent test instead of no test at all.
entries.effect: Results above 470 MHz are labelled, so a reader knows the rule was extended beyond the table.

entries.title: Where the signal is measured
entries.rule: The signal from a foreign station is worked out at several points along Finland's land border and the outer edge of its territorial sea, and the highest value is kept. Finnish stations that use the same channel are also checked at their own location.
entries.why: The strongest signal is not always at the closest point: a path over water carries much further than one over land. And the listed Finnish stations are where any harm would actually be felt.
entries.effect: Five spaced points are tested for each foreign station, and the highest value is the one reported.

entries.title: When nothing can be calculated
entries.rule: Three different outcomes are kept apart. A satellite that can never be seen from Finland is clear. A frequency band that has no applicable limit is recorded as having none. Only a filing that is missing the information needed is recorded as 'cannot calculate'.
entries.why: These mean very different things and must not look the same. A satellite Finland can't see cannot interfere. No limit means the rule doesn't apply. Missing information means we simply don't know, and a person should look.
entries.effect: Each of the three outcomes has its own place on the concern ladder.

entries.title: When two widths disagree
entries.rule: When a station's channel width and transmission width disagree, the smaller of the two is used.
entries.why: A disagreement like this is usually a typing error in the data. Always using the same rule keeps results consistent, and stops one mistake from creating overlaps that aren't really there.
entries.effect: The disagreement is flagged, and the smaller value is used.

entries.title: When a licence class is missing
entries.rule: A Finnish station with no licence class is recorded as 'other' (MUUT in the register). What the station transmits and receives decides the result, not its class.
entries.why: A missing label shouldn't remove a station from protection. What matters is how it uses the radio spectrum.
entries.effect: The station stays in the check, recorded as 'other'.

entries.title: Values that can't be right
entries.rule: Antenna gains above 60 dBi are not used, because no real antenna is that powerful. Stations whose position falls outside Finland's outline are kept, and flagged.
entries.why: One impossible value shouldn't decide a result. Leaving it out is safer than guessing what it should have been.
entries.effect: The station stays in the check; only the impossible value is ignored.

entries.title: Finnish use from the national frequency table
entries.rule: For every case over or near the level, Tosi lists the uses Finland's national frequency allocation table gives on the case's frequencies, and which of them are licence-exempt. The table is the annex to Traficom's Radio Frequency Regulation 4 (M4), taken from Traficom's open data.
entries.why: The list of stations to protect has no licence-exempt use, but being over the limit still matters where only licence-exempt equipment works. The table shows that use, so a person can judge the case.
entries.effect: The report cites the table's uses next to each case. The rung a case is on does not change.
basis: Traficom Radio Frequency Regulation 4 (M4), annex: national frequency allocation table
Traficom, 7 November 2026: over the limit counts even with only licence-exempt use

entries.title: The edge of the territorial sea is approximate
entries.rule: The outer edge of Finland's territorial sea is approximated as a line 12 nautical miles out from the coast, stopping halfway to neighbouring countries. It is not the official boundary.
entries.why: The official boundary is measured from base lines that aren't in Tosi's data. In some places it is narrower than this approximation, so results near the sea edge are approximate.
entries.effect: Any case that depends on this edge should be checked against the official boundary before acting on it.

entries.title: Some satellite plans are not checked
entries.rule: Filings made under the special satellite broadcasting plans (Appendices 30, 30A and 30B of the Radio Regulations) are not checked, because those plans are published outside the file Tosi reads.
entries.why: These plans have their own rules and their own publications. A clean result from Tosi says nothing about them.
entries.effect: Filings under these appendices need to be checked separately, for now.

entries.title: Limits that apply to named countries only
entries.rule: Some limits apply only to countries named in a footnote of the Radio Regulations. Those limits are not applied.
entries.why: The lists of countries in those footnotes aren't yet available in a structured form Tosi can read reliably.
entries.effect: If Finland is named in such a footnote, that limit will not be applied automatically; a person needs to check it.

entries.title: The wording of regulations isn't shown
entries.rule: Rules are referred to by their number, such as Article 21. The wording of the regulation itself is not shown in Tosi.
entries.why: The text of the regulations isn't included yet.
entries.effect: Anyone who needs the exact words has to open the Radio Regulations themselves.
